chunks: "Star grounding means that instead of chaining circuits along one ground wire, every circuit gets its own separate return path, and all of those paths meet at one single point, like spokes meeting at a hub.
The reason is that ground isn't really zero volts.

Any copper has resistance and inductance, so if a noisy circuit and a sensitive one share part of a return path, the noisy circuit's current creates a voltage drop that shows up in the sensitive circuit's reference.
In a star, the only shared point is the hub, so a motor drawing an amp doesn't move the reference of a sensor drawing a hundred microamps.
I'd typically put the star point at the power entry or the main bulk capacitor, and bring power-stage, digital and analog returns back to it separately.

The caveats are that it works best at low frequency, because the long legs are inductive at high frequency, and you have to avoid creating a second connection between the groups, like through a shield or scope ground, because that closes a ground loop.
On a PCB with a ground plane I usually create the star by placement rather than by cutting traces."
